updates.summary: Comprehensive federal order on AI safety and security. Under the Defense Production Act it directed the Secretary of Commerce to require companies developing potential dual-use foundation models to report on training, model-weight security and the results of red-team testing, with interim thresholds of 10^26 operations (10^23 for models trained mainly on biological sequence data) and for large computing clusters. It tasked NIST with guidelines and benchmarks for AI safety, red-teaming and evaluation, and directed agency action on synthetic-content labelling, critical infrastructure and cybersecurity, chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear risks, and federal use of AI.

updates.summary: California's frontier AI safety law. Large frontier developers must publish a frontier AI framework describing how they incorporate national and international standards and industry-consensus best practices, and must send the Office of Emergency Services summaries of their assessments of catastrophic risk from internal use of frontier models. The Office runs a mechanism for frontier developers and the public to report critical safety incidents. The Act protects whistleblowers who disclose significant risks posed by frontier models, creates a civil penalty enforced by the Attorney General, sets up the CalCompute consortium and has the Department of Technology recommend updates annually.
updates.notes: Signed 29 Sep 2025. Large frontier developers must send the Office of Emergency Services a summary of any assessment of catastrophic risk from internal use of their frontier models every three months or on another reasonable schedule they set (Business and Professions Code section 22757.12(d)); the Office runs a portal for these summaries and for critical safety incident reports. CalCompute is a consortium within the Government Operations Agency to develop a framework for a public computing cluster. The Governor's signing message says the Act provides a compliance pathway for the incident-reporting requirements if federal standards are adopted. Governor's EO N-9-26 (18 Sep 2026) seeks recommendations by 16 Nov 2026 on strengthening state law: independent verification of filings, onsite auditors, a 'kill switch', and loss-of-control incidents. The federal FRONTIER Act would preempt it.

updates.notes: Chapter 552 took effect on 1 Jan 2026. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority and must run an online complaint mechanism; the chapter gives no private right of action. Before suing, the Attorney General must give written notice and wait 60 days, during which the violation can be cured. Civil penalties are $10,000 to $12,000 for a curable violation, $80,000 to $200,000 for an uncurable one and $2,000 to $40,000 a day for a continuing one. A rebuttable presumption of reasonable care applies. A defendant is not liable if another person misuses the system, or if it discovers the violation through feedback, testing including red-teaming, state agency guidelines, or an internal review while substantially complying with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework Generative AI Profile or a comparable framework. State agencies may add sanctions of up to $100,000 against their licensees. Chapter 552 preempts local rules on AI.

updates.notes: Introduced 16 June 2022 (first reading); second reading and referral to the Standing Committee on Industry and Technology 24 April 2023, with a separate vote on Part 3; last committee meeting 26 Sept 2024. The Artificial Intelligence and Data Act would have come into force on a day or days fixed by order of the Governor in Council (its section 41). The 1st Session of the 44th Parliament was prorogued on 6 Jan 2025, and government bills without royal assent ceased to exist, so the bill died at committee stage. No AIDA successor as of Oct 2026: the June 2026 National AI Strategy relies on privacy and online-safety law modernisation instead. Bill C-36 (Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act, first reading 15 June 2026, sponsored by the Minister of AI and Digital Innovation) re-enacts only the privacy part of C-27, including disclosure on automated decision systems.

updates.official_identifier: Law No. 230-VIII ZRK (№ 230-VIII ЗРК) of 17 November 2025
updates.summary: Framework AI law. It defines an AI system as a digital object working on one or more AI models and sets principles including fairness, transparency and explainability, responsibility and controllability, priority of human well-being, and safety. Systems are classed by risk and by autonomy. It bans creating or operating systems with prohibited capabilities, among them manipulative or subliminal techniques, exploiting vulnerabilities, social scoring, biometric categorisation for discrimination and emotion recognition without consent. Owners and holders must manage risks; users must be told when goods or services use AI, and synthetic outputs must carry machine-readable labels.
updates.notes: Signed on 17 Nov 2025, together with a companion law amending other legislative acts on AI and digitalisation. That companion law aligns existing laws with the AI Law and also covers digital assets, personal-data consent and information security. Under Article 31 the law enters into force 60 calendar days after the day of its first official publication. Amended by Law No. 326-VIII of 24 Jun 2026 (Articles 1, 13, 17, 20 and 28), which also enters into force 60 calendar days after its first official publication. High-risk systems classed as critically important digital objects are treated like state systems for cybersecurity; sectoral agencies publish lists of trusted high-risk systems, for which an audit is required. Works created with AI are protected by copyright only where a human made a creative contribution, and works may be used for training only if the author or rightholder has not objected in machine-readable form.
